title: How do you decide whether a client should buy another company?
description: "Should the client buy this company?" A company buying another company (mergers and acquisitions).
hook: Decide whether a client should buy another company by testing four things in order: is the target a good business on its own, what extra is it worth to this buyer, can the buyer actually make the deal work, and is the price below the value. If standalone value plus realistic synergies, minus integration costs, beats the price, and buying beats building or partnering, the answer is yes.
body:
When you will use it

Any case where a company is thinking about buying a rival, a supplier, or a business with a market or capability it lacks: "Should our client buy X?" or "Is $60M a fair price for X?"

This is a decide question. You test the idea against a few yes/no questions, put a number on it and end with a clear yes or no, plus the conditions that would change your mind. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

Why does the client want to buy: growth, a capability, cost savings or a way into a new market?

The answer tells you what to test hardest: a deal done for cost savings lives or dies on the synergies; one done for a capability, on whether the people stay. Also ask whether the price quoted is for the whole business (enterprise value) or for the shares (equity value). The difference is the target's net debt.

The structure

  • Is the target good on its own?
    • Its market: size, growth, profitability
    • Its performance against peers
    • Standalone value: cash flows (DCF) or multiples of comparable deals
  • What extra is it worth to us?
    • Cost synergies (shared sites, purchasing, overheads)
    • Revenue synergies (cross-selling, new regions)
    • Minus one-off integration costs
  • Can we make it work?
    • Funding the deal
    • Integration and culture
    • Regulation (competition law)
  • Is the price right?
    • Price against value to us
    • Alternatives: another target, build it ourselves or partner

The rule that ties it together: buy only if standalone value + synergies − integration costs > price, and buying beats the alternatives. For the alternatives branch, see build, partner or buy.

A worked example: a bakery chain and a $60M rival

A regional bakery chain can buy a smaller rival for $60M (enterprise value, so debt is already accounted for). The case data, which is illustrative:

  • The rival earns $6M of EBITDA a year, and it is stable.
  • Similar bakery businesses have sold for about 8x EBITDA.
  • Management expects $3M a year of cost synergies from closing one bakery, buying flour jointly and merging head offices.
  • Integration (redundancy, IT, rebranding) costs $8M once.

Step 1: value the target on its own

$6M × 8 = $48M. The asking price is $12M above that, so the deal only makes sense if this buyer can earn synergies worth more than $12M.

Step 2: value the synergies, net of integration

Valuing $3M of annual savings at the same 8x multiple gives $24M. Subtract the $8M integration cost and the net synergy value is $16M. (Using the deal multiple is a shortcut. It ignores the year or two it takes to reach full savings, so say so out loud.)

Step 3: compare with the price

Value to this buyer is $48M + $16M = $64M, against a price of $60M. On paper the deal creates $4M. But look at who gets the benefit: the buyer pays $12M above standalone value, which hands the seller 75% of the $16M of net synergies.

Step 4: stress-test the synergies

If only half the cost savings arrive, the synergies are worth $1.5M × 8 = $12M, net $4M after integration. Value falls to $52M and the deal destroys $8M. The break-even point is $2.5M of annual savings, about 83% of plan. That is a thin margin of safety for savings that do not exist yet.

Revenue synergies are left out on purpose: they are less certain, so treat them as upside, not the reason to do the deal.

What a strong answer sounds like

"The rival is worth about $48M on its own, so at $60M we are paying $12M for synergies we have to deliver ourselves. Net of integration, the synergies are worth about $16M, so the deal works only if we hit at least 83% of the planned savings. I'd recommend bidding no more than about $52M to $55M, and walking away above $60M."

A weak answer says "There are good synergies, so I'd go ahead." It names no number and never says what price is too high.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting integration costs. Always subtract the one-off cost of combining the businesses.
  • Paying the seller for your own synergies. Every dollar of premium above standalone value gives away part of the buyer's own future work.
  • Mixing enterprise value and equity value. If the target has $10M of net debt and the $60M is the price for the shares, the buyer is really paying $70M for the business.
  • No downside case. Show what happens if synergies come in at half, and find the break-even level.
  • Forgetting the alternatives. A contract, a minority stake or building it yourself may give most of the benefit for less risk.

Practise it

1. A target earns $10M EBITDA. Comparable deals trade at 9x. Synergies are $2M a year and integration costs $6M. The seller wants $100M. What is the most the buyer should pay, and how sensitive is it?

Show the answer

Standalone: $10M × 9 = $90M. Synergies: $2M × 9 = $18M, minus $6M = $12M net. Value to the buyer: $102M, so $100M leaves only $2M of headroom. If synergies come in at 75% ($1.5M a year), they are worth $13.5M, net $7.5M, and value drops to $97.5M, below the price. The recommendation: bid well under $100M, or accept $100M only with strong evidence on the savings.

2. Should a coffee chain buy its main coffee roaster?

Show the answer
  • Value of the roaster: its profits, its other customers, price against value
  • Benefits to us: cheaper beans, secure supply, quality control
  • Risks: rival chains stop buying from a roaster we own; running a factory is a new skill
  • Alternatives: a long-term contract or a minority stake

Start with the alternatives: a long contract may give most of the benefit without buying. The trap is assuming ownership is the only way to secure supply.

Where to practise next

Read the complete guide to M&A cases and the short list of what to ask first in an M&A case. Then try a full case: PackRight (should a packaging maker buy a recycler?) or Tidewell Foods (is a snack brand worth $110M to us?). If the buyer is a fund, see how to structure a private equity case.
